In [[mathematics]], a '''Fatou–Bieberbach domain''' is a proper subdomain of <math>\mathbb{C}^n</math>, [[biholomorphic]]ally equivalent to  <math>\mathbb{C}^n</math>. That is, an open set <math>\Omega \subsetneq \mathbb{C}^n</math> is called a Fatou–Bieberbach domain if there exists a [[Biholomorphism|biholomorphic function]] <math>f:\Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^n</math> whose [[inverse function]] <math>f^{-1}:\mathbb{C}^n \rightarrow \Omega</math> is holomorphic.

== History ==
As a consequence of the [[Riemann mapping theorem]], there are no Fatou–Bieberbach domains in the case ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1.
[[Pierre Fatou]] and [[Ludwig Bieberbach]] first explored such domains in  higher dimensions in the 1920s, hence the name given to them later. Since the 1980s, Fatou–Bieberbach domains have again become the subject of mathematical research.

== Examples ==

Fatou–Bieberbach domains occur in great numbers for <math>n\ge 2</math>.

Let <math>\operatorname{Aut}\left(\mathbb{C}^n\right)</math> denote the group of biholomorphisms of type <math>\mathbb C^n \to \mathbb C^n</math>. [[Basins of attraction|Basins of attractions]] produce many FB domains, according to the following theorem. 

{{Math theorem
| name = Theorem
| note = {{Harvard citation|Rosay|Rudin|1988}}
| math_statement = Suppose that <math display="inline">F \in \operatorname{Aut}\left(\mathbb{C}^n\right)</math> fixes a point <math display="inline">p \in \mathbb{C}^n</math> and that all eigenvalues <math display="inline">\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n</math> of <math display="inline">F^{\prime}(p)</math> satisfy <math display="inline">\left|\lambda_i\right|<1</math>. Let <math display="inline">\Omega</math> be the set of all <math display="inline">z \in \mathbb{C}^n</math> for which <math display="inline">\lim _{k \rightarrow \infty} F^k(z)=p</math> where <math display="inline">F^k=F \circ F^{k-1}, F^1=F</math>. Then there exists a biholomorphic map <math display="inline">\Psi</math> from <math display="inline">\Omega</math> onto <math display="inline">\mathbb{C}^n</math>.
}}

* Let <math>A\in GL(n,\mathbb C)</math> with spectral radius <math>\rho(A)<1</math>. Set <math>F(z)=Az</math>. This is a contraction map with basin <math>\Omega=\mathbb C^n</math>.
* In <math>\mathbb C^2</math>, let <math>F_a(z,w)=(\,w+z^2,\ a z\,)</math> with <math>0<|a|<1</math>. Then <math>F_a^{-1}(z,w)=(\,w/a,\ z-(w/a)^2\,)</math>. It has two fixed points: <math>(0, 0), (1-a, a(1-a))</math>. The point <math>p=(0,0)</math> is fixed and <math>F_a'(0)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ a&0\end{pmatrix}</math> has eigenvalues <math>\pm\sqrt{a}</math>. The basin <math>\Omega=\{(z,w): F_a^k(z,w)\to(0,0)\}</math> is a proper [[Open set|open subset]] of <math>\mathbb C^2</math> and thus a Fatou–Bieberbach domain.

* More generally, for <math>F(z,w)=(\,w+P(z),\ a z\,)</math>, where <math>0<|a|<1</math>, and <math>P</math> a polynomial with all monomials having degree at least 2. The basin of attraction of <math>0</math> is a Fatou–Bieberbach domain in <math>\mathbb C^2</math>. These maps are called complex [[Hénon map|Hénon maps]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fornæss |first1=John Erik |last2=Sibony |first2=Nessim |date=1992-02-01 |title=Complex Hénon mappings in ℂ2 and Fatou-Bieberbach domains |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/duke-mathematical-journal/volume-65/issue-2/Complex-H%c3%a9non-mappings-in-%e2%84%822-and-Fatou-Bieberbach-domains/10.1215/S0012-7094-92-06515-X.full |journal=Duke Mathematical Journal |volume=65 |issue=2 |doi=10.1215/S0012-7094-92-06515-X |issn=0012-7094|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
More generally, for any <math>F \in \operatorname{Aut}\left(\mathbb{C}^n\right)</math> and any atttractive fixed point <math>p</math>, let <math>\Omega</math> be its basin of attraction. If <math>\Omega</math> is not all of <math>\mathbb C^n</math>, then it is a Fatou–Bieberbach domain. It is also a [[Runge domain|Runge subset]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Forstnerič |first1=F. |last2=Kutzschebauch |first2=F. |date=2022-06-01 |title=The First Thirty Years of Andersén-Lempert Theory |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10476-022-0130-1 |journal=Analysis Mathematica |language=en |volume=48 |issue=2 |pages=489–544 |doi=10.1007/s10476-022-0130-1 |arxiv=2111.08802 |issn=1588-273X}}</ref> It was an [[open problem]] for a long time whether there exists Fatou–Bieberbach domains that are not Runge. This was answered in the affirmative in 2008.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wold |first=Erlend Fornæss |date=2008-04-01 |title=A Fatou–Bieberbach domain in $$\mathbb {C}^2$$which is not Runge |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00208-007-0168-1 |journal=Mathematische Annalen |language=en |volume=340 |issue=4 |pages=775–780 |doi=10.1007/s00208-007-0168-1 |issn=1432-1807|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Let <math>L_1, L_2, \dots</math> be countably many complex-[[Affine space|affine subspaces]] of <math>\mathbb C^n</math>. There exists a Fatou–Bieberbach domain <math>\Omega</math> such that <math>L_j \cap \Omega</math> is a connected proper subset of <math>L_j</math> for all <math>j</math>.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Wold |first=Erlend FornæSs |date=November 2005 |title=Fatou–Bieberbach domains |url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/S0129167X05003235 |journal=International Journal of Mathematics |language=en |volume=16 |issue=10 |pages=1119–1130 |doi=10.1142/S0129167X05003235 |issn=0129-167X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Given countably many [[Algebraic variety|closed subvarieties]] of <math>\mathbb C^n</math>. There exists a Fatou–Bieberbach domain <math>\Omega</math> that contains all of them.<ref name=":1" />

The boundary of a Fatou–Bieberbach can be very wild. For any <math>k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \infty\} </math> there exists <math>k </math> disjoint Fatou–Bieberbach domains <math>\Omega_1, \Omega_2, \dots, \Omega_k </math>, such that <math>\forall z \in \mathbb C^n \setminus\cap_{j=1}^k \Omega_j </math>, <math>z </math> is on the boundary of all <math>\Omega_j </math>. Similar to [[lakes of Wada]].<ref name=":1" />

The Andersén–Lempert theorem states that the group generated by shearing maps is dense in <math>\operatorname{Aut}\left(\mathbb{C}^n\right)</math>. This allows construction of many Fatou–Bieberbach domains.<ref name=":0" />

== Properties ==
No Fatou–Bieberbach domain is bounded, since a bounded image of an entire map <math>\mathbb C^n\to\Omega</math> would violate [[Liouville's theorem (complex analysis)|Liouville's theorem]] componentwise.

By the [[Ax–Grothendieck theorem]], if <math>\Omega</math> is Fatou–Bieberbach, then for any biholomorphism <math>f:\Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^n</math>, <math>f^{-1}</math> is not a polynomial.

Biholomorphism preserves Fatou–Bieberbach domains. That is, if <math>\Psi\in\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb C^n)</math> and <math>\Omega</math> is Fatou–Bieberbach, then <math>\Psi(\Omega)</math> is Fatou–Bieberbach.

In one dimension, there are no Fatou–Bieberbach domains, due to [[Picard's great theorem]].

{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof= 
Let <math>\Omega\subset\mathbb C</math> be open, and <math>\phi:\Omega\to\mathbb C</math> be biholomorphic. Then <math>F=\phi^{-1}:\mathbb C\to\Omega</math> is entire and injective. If <math>\infty</math> were an essential singularity of <math>F</math>, Picard implies <math>F</math> is dense near every value with at most one exception, contradicting injectivity. Hence <math>\infty</math> is a pole or removable, so <math>F</math> is polynomial. Since it is injective, it must be affine <math>F(z)=az+b</math> with <math>a \neq 0</math>, so <math>\Omega = \mathbb C</math>.
}}

Being biholomorphic to <math>\mathbb C^n</math>, every Fatou–Bieberbach domain is a [[Stein manifold]] and a [[domain of holomorphy]].

For any <math>\Omega \subset \mathbb C^n</math> that is both Runge and Fatou–Bieberbach, for any <math>p \in \Omega</math>, there exists a sequence of biholomorphisms <math>f_1, f_2, \dots : \mathbb C^n \to \mathbb C^n</math> such that they all fix <math>p</math>, and <math>\Omega = \{z \in \mathbb C^n : \lim_{k \to \infty} f_k \circ\cdots \circ f_1 (z) = p\}</math><ref name=":1" />
